conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us see whether you might be experiencing postpartum depression or anxiety, and it includes one question about self-harm. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team; none of it will affect your care unless you choose to include others. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause or clarify anything you need.

Whenever you’re ready, here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[lets out a small sigh]  
Honestly, most of the time it feels pretty difficult. I can still smile if someone shows me a cute baby video or if my husband makes a little joke, but it’s like the laughter just doesn’t come easily anymore. I’ll think “that’s funny,” but the actual laughing part feels kind of… flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow head-shake]  
No… not really. I mean, I try—sometimes I’ll force a little chuckle when my husband jokes around—but it feels fake, like I’m just going through the motions. Nothing feels genuinely funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quietly]  
Not much… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now it all feels like another chore. I still go, because I know I *should*, but that spark of “I can’t wait” just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to the floor, voice tight]  
Yeah… pretty much every day. If the baby spits up more than usual, I immediately think it’s because I ate something “wrong.” When he wouldn’t settle last night, I kept telling myself it’s because I’m not doing something right, that a “good mom” would know how to calm him. I know, rationally, babies just cry—but I still feel like it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands in lap]  
Yes… a lot of the time. I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart races because I’m sure he’s not breathing—even though I can see his chest moving. Or I’ll lie awake imagining he’ll choke on spit-up the second I close my eyes. There’s no real reason, but the worry keeps looping anyway.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[nods slowly, voice shaky]  
Yeah… it hits out of nowhere. Like yesterday, I was folding his laundry and suddenly felt this wave of terror—my chest got tight, I couldn’t catch my breath, and I had to sit down on the floor. Nothing had happened, but for a minute I was convinced something awful was about to happen to him… or to me.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily]  
Most of the time. Even little stuff—like the dishes piling up or figuring out what’s for dinner—feels huge. I’ll look at the mess and think, “I can’t do this,” then cry while I’m scrubbing bottles because it all feels too heavy. I manage the basics, but it’s like I’m constantly one step away from drowning.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quietly]  
Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop. I replay every little thing I did that day, worrying I held him wrong or didn’t burp him long enough. Then I’m scared to fall too deep in case he needs me, so I jerk awake at every tiny noise. A few nights this week I’ve only gotten maybe three broken hours.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes well up]  
Pretty much all the time. I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling that just sticks to me. I’ll look at his little face and feel like I should be glowing, but instead there’s this constant ache in my chest. I keep wondering if I’m already failing him.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Voice cracks, tears start]  
Yeah... it's been like that a few times this week. I'll just be rocking him and suddenly the tears come. Or I'll be in the shower where no one can see and just sob. It feels like the sadness just builds up until it spills out. Sometimes I don't even know exactly why I'm crying, just that I can't seem to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No—no, I could never. I’ve felt low, but hurting myself never crossed my mind. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant <12 wks  

A. Self-Reported Symptoms (verbatim themes)  
- Persistent low mood, “heavy gray feeling,” daily tearfulness  
- Marked anhedonia: no genuine pleasure in social or usual activities  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care; “I’m already failing him”  
- Recurrent, intrusive worries about infant safety; panic attacks without precipitant  
- Overwhelmed by routine tasks; describes “drowning” under minor demands  
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia, middle-waking related to rumination & hypervigilance  

B. Observed / Expressed Behaviours  
- Tearful during interview; hand-wringing; avoids eye contact when describing guilt  
- Maintains strong attachment to infant; denies thoughts of self-harm  

C. Screening Risk Indicators  
- Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale analogue: ≥9 affirmative low-mood / anxiety items  
- Absence of suicidal ideation (explicitly denied)  
- High functional impairment (household tasks, social withdrawal)  

D. Summary Statement  
Screening reveals significant postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms with impaired daily functioning. No current self-harm ideation. Recommend formal diagnostic assessment, consideration of perinatal mood disorder, and safety planning given rapid symptom escalation.
